variables_rover_strings.text: The rover's slope variable. No global product has a 300 m baseline: it is read from the isotropic km-baseline slope (see true_baseline).

Every slope variable the missions name (rover slope_300m_deg and solar slope_deg, both aliased to slope_deg) is read from the isotropic-baseline column instead, on both bodies. The literal slope_deg uses a one-pixel east-west spacing that shrinks as cos(latitude), so near the poles the east-west baseline falls to tens of metres and inflates the slope; both builders documented this (provenance rows of slope_deg, slope_p90_deg and slope_iso_deg). slope_iso_deg keeps the same baseline in both directions at every latitude (true baseline read from the provenance row). Equal to slope_deg at low latitudes.

Every slope variable the missions name (rover slope_300m_deg and solar slope_deg, both aliased to slope_deg) is read from the isotropic-baseline column instead, on both bodies. The literal slope_deg uses a one-pixel east-west spacing that shrinks as cos(latitude), so near the poles the east-west baseline falls to tens of metres and inflates the slope; both builders documented this (provenance rows of slope_deg, slope_p90_deg and slope_iso_deg). slope_iso_deg keeps the same baseline in both directions at every latitude (true baseline read from the provenance row). Equal to slope_deg at low latitudes.

Not a 300 m slope. km-baseline slopes are much gentler than rover-scale slopes; a 15 deg gate means something different here. slope_p90_deg is the steeper tail. Poleward of ~85 deg the literal 1-pixel east-west spacing shrinks to metres and inflates slope_deg/slope_p90_deg; slope_iso_deg/slope_iso_p90_deg (3.79 km baseline in both directions) are the reliable values there.
The rover's roughness variable. RMS height difference (deviogram) at a lag of about 1.9 km, not 300 m (see true_baseline).
